title: VKH Syndrome: The Definitive Clinical Guide
summary: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is a multisystemic autoimmune disorder characterized by bilateral granulomatous panuveitis involving the eyes, ears, meninges, and skin. It is driven by T-cell mediated destruction of melanocytes in genetically susceptible individuals.

sections.title: 1. Clinical Definition & Scope
sections.content: Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada (VKH) syndrome is an idiopathic multisystem autoimmune disease directed against melanocyte-associated antigens (tyrosinase, TRP1, TRP2). It manifests as a bilateral, diffuse, granulomatous panuveitis often associated with exudative retinal detachments, neurological (meningismus), auditory (tinnitus/dysacusis), and integumentary (vitiligo/poliosis) signs.

sections.title: 4. The Four Clinical Stages
content: Step 1: Prodromal Stage (Days) — Mimics viral illness; headache, meningismus, tinnitus, CSF pleocytosis.
Step 2: Acute Uveitic Stage (Weeks) — Sudden bilateral vision loss; multifocal exudative RD, optic disc edema, thickened choroid.
Step 3: Convalescent Stage (Months) — Depigmentation; 'Sunset Glow Fundus', Sugiura sign (perilimbal vitiligo), integumentary vitiligo.
Step 4: Chronic Recurrent Stage — Smoldering granulomatous anterior uveitis; Mutton-fat KPs, Busacca nodules, Iris bombe/Glaucoma.

sections.title: 5. Extraocular Manifestations
content: Neurological: Headache, stiff neck, meningeal signs, CSF pleocytosis (>90% in acute stage).
Auditory: Tinnitus, dysacusis, vertigo, high-frequency hearing loss.
Integumentary: Vitiligo (patchy depigmentation), Poliosis (whitening of lashes/hair), Alopecia.

rows: No hx trauma/surgery + Bilateral ocular involvement + Neurological/Auditory signs + Integumentary signs.
No hx trauma/surgery + Bilateral ocular involvement + EITHER Neurological/Auditory OR Integumentary signs.
No hx trauma/surgery + Bilateral ocular involvement ONLY (Isolated Ocular Disease).

sections.title: 8. Multimodal Imaging Pearls
content: FFA: Early pinpoint 'starry sky' leakage, late pooling in subretinal spaces (flower-petal pattern).
ICGA: Hypofluorescent dark spots (HDLs) representing granulomas; delayed choroidal filling.
EDI-OCT: Massive diffuse choroidal thickening (>600-800 microns) in acute stage.
B-Scan: Low-to-medium internal reflectivity choroidal thickening; absence of posterior scleritis signs.

sections.title: 10. Management Protocol
content: Phase 1: Induction — IV Methylprednisolone (1g/day for 3 days) or high-dose oral Prednisone (1.0–1.5 mg/kg).
Phase 2: Slow Taper — Very gradual oral steroid reduction over 6-9 months; do NOT taper faster than 5-10mg/month.
Phase 3: IMT — Early introduction of Mycophenolate Mofetil (1g BID) or Azathioprine to reduce recurrence.
Phase 4: Biologics — Adalimumab or Infliximab for refractory cases failing traditional IMT.

sections.title: 11. Red Flags & Emergencies
content: Rapid tapering of steroids (Primary cause of recurrence)
Development of CNVM (Requires Anti-VEGF)
Secondary Glaucoma (Pupillary block or steroid-induced)
Neurological deterioration despite therapy

content.explanation: S: Sunset glow fundus, K: KPs (mutton-fat), I: Integumentary (Vitiligo/Poliosis), N: Neurological/Noise (Tinnitus).

sections.title: 13. Ocular Complications
content: Cataract: Most common complication (40-50%).
Glaucoma: Angle-closure (ciliary body edema) or Steroid-response.
Subretinal Fibrosis: Occurs in chronic phase; poor visual prognosis.
CNVM: Juxtafoveal choroidal neovascular membranes.

sections.title: 14. Landmark Study: Steroids vs. IMT
sections.content: Recent evidence (e.g., studies by Abu El-Asrar et al.) suggests that early aggressive combined therapy (Steroids + Mycophenolate Mofetil) leads to better long-term visual outcomes and a lower rate of progression to the 'Sunset Glow' stage compared to steroid monotherapy.

sections.title: 15. Clinical Pearls for Rounds
content: Sugiura Sign: Perilimbal vitiligo, the earliest depigmentation sign (often within 1 month).
The 3-Month Rule: Most recurrences happen when Prednisone is tapered below 20mg within the first 3 months.
CSF Pleocytosis: May be present even if the patient has no meningeal symptoms.
Dalen-Fuchs Nodules: Not pathognomonic; seen in VKH, Sarcoid, and Sympathetic Ophthalmia.
